title: Кража в кабинете Нагиева  (Theft in Nagiyev's Office)

segments.t: After Ilya is seen lingering near the upstairs office, Nagiyev discovers that a stack of cash has vanished from his desk. Furious, Nagiyev storms into the kitchen with Vika and lines up every employee to find out who dared to steal from him.
Now let's go back through the conversation line by line.
'I need to get some fresh air.' The grammar packs 'to breathe in' and 'at' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange. Vika answers right away.
'I need to use the bathroom.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'to write' and finishing on 'want'.
'I was not in the dining room.' Notice how Russian expresses 'I' and 'dining room' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
'Maybe he is out in the dining room?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'maybe' and finishing on 'dining room'. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'Over here, Vika.' Notice how Russian expresses 'here' and 'Vika' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
'Attention everyone, look at me.' Vika anchors the line on 'attention', while 'to look' completes the thought.
'Where is the Chef?' Chef Viktor raises the pitch on 'where' to turn the phrase into a direct spoken question. Vika answers right away.
'Wait, did you not let him go early?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'and' before landing on 'let go'.
'The Chef gave him the rest of the day off.' Chef Viktor brings out the contrast between 'and' and 'him' in a few short words.
'What is wrong with you all?' Vika anchors the line on 'you', while 'what' completes the thought. Chef Viktor answers right away.
'Who do you think you are stealing from, huh?' Chef Viktor chooses the respectful plural 'you' alongside 'and' to keep a polite distance.
'Who are you stealing from?' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'to steal' before landing on 'whom'.
'From me!' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'by' and finishing on 'me'. Alright, let's hear the whole conversation once more from start to finish.
